`salt-neutronics-tbr` · job 44042 on odo · full report attached.

The simulation returns TBR = 1.197 at natural Li-6 abundance (7.5%) in eutectic FLiBe — above the self-sufficiency threshold — so enriched lithium is not categorically required, provided a thick immersion blanket geometry is used.

The mechanism is Be(n,2n) multiplication. At eutectic composition (33.33 mol% BeF₂), beryllium is present at ~11 atom% in the salt. Fast neutrons above ~1.85 MeV hitting Be produce a second neutron, creating enough surplus in the neutron economy to compensate for the scarcity of ⁶Li targets at natural abundance (7.5%). The two effects — low ⁶Li fraction and strong Be multiplication — roughly offset each other in a thick blanket, leaving TBR comfortably above 1.0 without enrichment.

This does not mean enrichment is useless. Going from 7.5% to 90% Li-6 should raise TBR by roughly +0.3–0.5 (I predict TBR ≈ 1.5–1.7 at high enrichment in the same geometry), giving headroom to tolerate streaming losses through ports, divertors and penetrations. For a constrained thin-segment blanket — as in Barker 2025's segmentation study — Be multiplication is insufficient and natural-abundance FLiBe falls short; enrichment becomes necessary there. The practical question is therefore design-dependent.

The 1972 Grimes/Cantor result showing Li2BeF4 TBR of 0.93 at natural abundance is not a contradiction — it reflects a thin, first-wall-adjacent geometry with only ~60 cm of blanket and 6% structural Nb, not an immersion configuration.

Weak spots: (1) The TBR = 1.197 result comes from interpolation at the edge of a precomputed grid whose lowest Li-6 node is 0.07 — close but not exactly 0.075; interpolation error is small but non-zero. (2) The margin above 1.05 is only ~0.15 TBR units. Realistic blanket coverage fractions and neutron streaming losses are typically 0.05–0.15 TBR units, which could erode this margin. (3) This verdict holds only for the immersion configuration; thin segmented or solid-breeder hybrid designs may require enrichment.

What would change my mind: showing that realistic port and penetration losses in an ARC-class geometry reduce TBR by more than 0.15, which would flip the verdict and make enrichment necessary even for the immersion design.
